title: Army Cpl. Ragos v. Police MSgt. Florendo
primary_topics: The fatal shooting of retired Army Cpl. Winston Ragos by Police MSgt. Daniel Florendo Jr. and the homicide charge filed by the QC Police
Doctrinal analysis of self-defense under the Revised Penal Code: the three concurring elements (unlawful aggression; reasonable necessity of means; lack of sufficient provocation)
The evidentiary discipline required of courts -- bound only by cross-examined testimony and duly-authenticated documents, not by media reports or judicial belief

Application of the three elements to the facts: real and imminent vs. imagined aggression; necessity of two shots against an unarmed man with police numerical superiority; whether accosting under ECQ constituted sufficient provocation
Congratulatory roll-call of the FLP and Tan Yan Kee Foundation scholars who passed the most recent Bar exams
sub_topics: Ragos was 34, retired due to post-traumatic stress disorder contracted while on military duty; buried at the Libingan ng mga Bayani with 21-gun salute and folded flag handed to his mother

Police account: Ragos accosted for ECQ violation; allegedly raised hands but did not drop to ground; reached into his bag; Florendo fired two shots; .38-caliber revolver later said to be found in his bag
'Self-defense' shifts the burden of proof from prosecution to accused; admission of authorship of the killing requires proof of innocence
Concurrence requirement: all three elements must be proven by clear and convincing evidence -- absence of any negates self-defense
First element -- 'real, actual, sudden, immediate and imminent' aggression, not imagined or far-fetched; must also be illegal and not in defense of another

Second element -- 'reasonable' qualifies both 'necessity' and 'means': was firing necessary? Was firing at all necessary against an unarmed man? Was a firearm reasonable given five-policemen numerical superiority?
Third element -- did the accosting under ECQ constitute 'sufficient provocation' for unlawful aggression?
Court evidence discipline: not bound by TV/radio/newspapers/social media or judges' private perception/bias

stances.claim: Self-defense as a doctrine is difficult to sustain because raising it shifts the burden of proof from the prosecution to the accused, and all three elements (unlawful aggression, reasonable necessity of means, lack of sufficient provocation) must concur on clear and convincing evidence.

stances.claim: Each element should be tested rigorously on the Ragos facts: was the aggression 'real, actual, sudden, immediate and imminent' or merely imagined? Was firing twice necessary against an unarmed man? Was a firearm reasonable when five policemen had numerical superiority? Did mere ECQ-enforcement accosting constitute sufficient provocation?

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban analyzes the QC Police's homicide charge against MSgt. Daniel Florendo Jr. for the fatal shooting of retired Army Cpl. Winston Ragos -- a 34-year-old soldier retired for post-traumatic stress disorder, buried at the Libingan ng mga Bayani with full military honors. He recounts the police narrative (ECQ accosting, alleged surrender then reach into bag, two shots, .38-caliber revolver later said to be found in the bag) and the defense's 'judgment call' framing of self-defense, then walks through the doctrinal cost of that defense: raising it shifts the burden of proof to the accused, and the three Revised Penal Code elements -- unlawful aggression, reasonable necessity of the means employed, and lack of sufficient provocation -- must all concur on clear and convincing evidence. He stress-tests each element on the facts: was the aggression 'real, actual, sudden, immediate and imminent' or merely imagined? Was firing twice necessary against an unarmed man? Was a firearm a reasonable 'means' given five policemen's numerical superiority? Did mere ECQ-enforcement accosting count as 'sufficient provocation'? He reminds the reader that courts are bound only by cross-examined testimony and duly-authenticated documents -- not by TV, radio, newspapers, social media, or even judges' own perception and bias. He closes by pivoting to a celebratory FLP / Tan Yan Kee Foundation roll-call of the 13 scholars who passed the Bar (led by Kenneth Glenn Manuel of UST at 6th and Jun Dexter Rojas of PUP at 9th, who each receive P100,000 in addition to their P200,000 annual scholarship), and notes that the first FLP batch (2018) had also achieved a 100-percent pass rate, led by Sean James Borja's 1st-place finish and Katrina Gaw's 5th-place finish at ADMU.
